extracted.intended_audience: Writers (including LIS authors) interested in submitting humor/satire to McSweeney's Internet Tendency
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for writing and submitting short humor/satire pieces to McSweeney's Internet Tendency (website and e-newsletter), with notes aimed at LIS authors on tone, length, and audience fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission length
rubrics_metrics.description: “Submissions should be shortish. By shortish we mean an absolute maximum of 1,200 words, but in truth we veer toward pieces that are under 1,000 words, and snuggle closest to ones that are even shorter than that.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concise pieces (well under 1,000 words where possible). Longer pieces up to 1,200 words are the absolute maximum. For LIS authors, convey concepts in small, precise ways rather than long academic treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of contributions accepted
rubrics_metrics.description: All types of submissions are allowed. Lists, open letters to people who are unlikely to respond, monologues, food reviews, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be inventive — lists, imagined monologues, food reviews, open letters and similar short comedic formats are explicitly welcome. The publication values a wide variety of short-form comedic approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission method: paste into email; no attachments or links
rubrics_metrics.description: “Please paste the entire document into the email message. Please don’t share Google docs or links to your private blogs. Also, very important: do not send us attachments.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put the full text in the body of the email (not as attachments or external links). Sending attachments, Google Doc links, or private-blog links is an anti-pattern and risks automatic rejection or not being read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not send the same submission to multiple addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: The website notes DO NOT send the same submission to multiple addresses, it is unnecessary as it all goes to the same editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cross-posting the same piece to multiple McSweeney's inboxes; it clutters editorial workflow and is discouraged. Use the appropriate inbox for the piece type instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the correct dedicated inbox for piece type
rubrics_metrics.description: There are separate email addresses depending on the nature of your submission (websubmissions@mcsweeneys.net; timelysubmissions@mcsweeneys.net; lists@mcsweeneys.net; openletters@mcsweeneys.net; newfood@mcsweeneys.net).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the inbox that matches your piece type (lists, open letters, new food reviews, timely pieces). This helps routing and editor consideration. Note: despite multiple addresses, one editor reads submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness requirement for 'timely' inbox
rubrics_metrics.description: Timely submissions should be sent to timelysubmissions@mcsweeneys.net. This inbox is for super topical pieces riffing on big news stories of the last 24-48 hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely pieces must be topical and fresh—aim to riff on news within a 24–48 hour window. Slow-to-arrive topical pieces will not fit this category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title/subject-line must reveal premise and be eye-catching
rubrics_metrics.description: “We get hundreds of submissions a week and, like we have mentioned, there’s just one editor reading them all. So, it’s only natural that this editor will be drawn to submissions with funny, eye-catching titles that cleverly reveal the premises of pieces.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a funny, eye-catching title/subject line that clearly signals your piece's premise—this increases the chance the single editor will open and read it. Avoid vague or misleading subject lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial tone and purpose: entertain with comedic/satirical voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Content is intended to be humorous/satire. The purpose of such pieces should ultimately be to entertain the reader, rather than function as straightforward articles on an LIS-related issue. Editorial tone: Light and comedic/satirical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize comedic voice, satire, and entertainment value over instructional or academic explanation. Even pieces rooted in LIS topics should have a comedic edge and aim to amuse rather than inform in an academic way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting/style: keep it ordinary/plain
rubrics_metrics.description: “Please do not format your piece in an unusual way. Do not use colors or fun fonts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard, plain email/text formatting. Avoid unusual layouts, color text, or decorative fonts. Unconventional formatting is discouraged and may hinder consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience fit: literary, high-brow satirical readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers are intelligent, open minded, literary, and comfortable thinking outside of the box, especially in a satirical way. The publication “delivers its humor in a high-brow lit mag sort of way.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target readers who appreciate literary/ironic satire and cleverness. Tailor voice and references to a well-read, literate audience rather than purely lowbrow gag-jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical editorial reality: high volume and single-editor bottleneck
rubrics_metrics.description: “We get hundreds of submissions a week and, like we have mentioned, there’s just one editor reading them all.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of high submission volume and limited editorial capacity, pieces should be immediately engaging (strong title/premise), concise, and easy to read. Stand-out originality helps; expect an informal, non-peer-reviewed selection process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform and medium suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Type: Civilian publication. Medium: Website and e-newsletter. Frequency of publication: Daily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write pieces suited to web consumption and e-newsletter distribution—short, punchy, and quickly digestible material works best. Daily publication cadence favors timely, concise submissions.
